title: [v3-4-test] Enforce execution_timeout for tasks run by a language SDK (#74869)
body:
* Extract a helper that looks up the stub task

* Add execution_timeout to TIRunContext

* Add execution_timeout to the supervisor schema

* Arm the supervisor execution timeout from the run context

* Document that the supervisor timeout covers language SDK tasks

* Treat a negative execution_timeout as elapsed for language SDK tasks

The Python task runner fails a task with a negative execution_timeout
right away. Sent as-is, a negative value would instead move the
supervisor's SIGTERM deadline to an arbitrary earlier point, and
treating it as no timeout would let the task run forever. Clamping it
to zero makes the supervisor treat the timeout as already elapsed,
which is the closest the outside layer can get to the Python behavior.

* Send execution_timeout in the run context for all tasks

* Start the execution timeout for language SDK tasks in the coordinator

* Replace SetExecutionTimeout with StartExecutionTimeout

* Look up the task once in ti_run

* Fill the default execution_timeout of Lang-SDK tasks from the config

* Arm the execution timeout only in _arm_execution_timeout

* Store execution_timeout at startup and arm it in _on_child_started

* Align docstrings with the execution timeout changes

* Rename the task variable in ti_run to fix mypy
(cherry picked from commit 597aff10d71ca8e02de97d891e4f758c878bb1f7)

Co-authored-by: ChickenBenny <zxc123benny14159@gmail.com>

@@ -140,10 +140,10 @@ Timeouts
 If you want a task to have a maximum runtime, set its ``execution_timeout`` attribute to a ``datetime.timedelta`` value
 that is the maximum permissible runtime. This applies to all Airflow tasks, including sensors. ``execution_timeout`` controls the
 maximum time allowed for every execution. If ``execution_timeout`` is breached, the task times out and
-``AirflowTaskTimeout`` is raised. For tasks executed by the Python task runner, the task supervisor enforces
-the timeout from outside the task process too: if the task has not stopped within ``[core] killed_task_cleanup_time``
-seconds after ``execution_timeout`` elapses (for example because it is blocked in native code that never returns
-control to Python), the supervisor sends it SIGTERM, and SIGKILL after the same period again.
+``AirflowTaskTimeout`` is raised. The task supervisor also enforces the timeout from outside the task process:
+if the task has not stopped within ``[core] killed_task_cleanup_time`` seconds after ``execution_timeout`` elapses
+(for example because it is blocked in native code), the supervisor sends it SIGTERM, and SIGKILL after the same
+period again. Tasks run by a language SDK do not raise ``AirflowTaskTimeout`` and are stopped only this way.
 
 In addition, sensors have a ``timeout`` parameter. This only matters for sensors in ``reschedule`` mode. ``timeout`` controls the maximum
 time allowed for the sensor to succeed. If ``timeout`` is breached, ``AirflowSensorTimeout`` will be raised and the sensor fails immediately

+def get_task(dag_bag: DBDagBag, ti: Any, *, session: Session) -> SerializedOperator | None:
+    """Return the task of *ti* from its Dag version, or ``None`` if it cannot be found."""
+    if ti.dag_version_id is None:
+        return None
+    if (dag := dag_bag.get_dag(ti.dag_version_id, session=session)) is None:

+def get_arg_bindings(task: SerializedOperator | None) -> list | None:
     """
-    Extract the stub task's TaskFlow arg spec from its Dag version.
+    Return the TaskFlow arg spec of *task* if it is a stub task.
 
     Mapped (``.expand()``) stubs never capture a parse-time spec, so they resolve to
     ``None`` here and keep the legacy ignored-args behavior; per-map-index delivery
     lands in a follow-up.
     """
-    if ti.dag_version_id is None:
-        return None
-    if (dag := dag_bag.get_dag(ti.dag_version_id, session=session)) is None:
-        return None
-    if (task := dag.task_dict.get(ti.task_id)) is None or not task.is_stub:
+    if task is None or not task.is_stub:
         return None
     return task.arg_bindings
+
+
+def get_execution_timeout(task: SerializedOperator | None) -> float | None:
+    """
+    Return the ``execution_timeout`` of *task* in seconds.
+
+    Like the Python task runner, a zero timeout means no timeout, and a negative one has
+    already elapsed.
+    """
+    if task is None or not task.execution_timeout:
+        return None
+    return max(task.execution_timeout.total_seconds(), 0.0)
